Description_en: Every Change Has a Way Back
Body_en:
Kooboo History & Deployment

Every Change Has a Way Back

Compare, undo, restore, test, package, and publish from the same Web OS.

Building a website is easy when nothing changes.

Real work is different. A developer edits a layout. A content manager changes a page. AI updates several objects. A new version is tested. Production receives the change. Then someone discovers that yesterday’s behavior was better.

Traditional web stacks divide this lifecycle across source control, database backups, deployment scripts, file-transfer tools, staging servers, CMS revisions, and hosting dashboards. Each system knows one part of the story. Restoring the complete application means reconstructing that story under pressure.

Kooboo treats change history, website objects, testing environments, portability, and remote publishing as parts of the same platform.

A production system should make change fast—but recovery faster.

Demo one: change a page, compare it, and undo it

Begin with a working website and make a visible change:

  1. Edit a heading and one section of a page.
  2. Open the website history.
  3. Find the corresponding edit-log item.
  4. Compare the recorded version with the latest version.
  5. Undo the change.
  6. Refresh the website and show the restored result.

Undo in Kooboo is itself a new change. The platform does not need to erase the historical record to move the object back. The recovery action becomes part of the history that follows it.

Demo two: publish the same website to another Kooboo server

Deployment should demonstrate application movement, not only a copied HTML page.

  1. Configure a remote Kooboo destination.
  2. Publish the current website changes.
  3. Show the pages, layouts, views, scripts, styles, data, and routes operating on the destination.
  4. Make another local change and publish only the new log items.
  5. Create an intentional conflict and show Kooboo stopping with both sides available for review.

History belongs to the website object

A CMS revision system often remembers only page text. That is not enough for a dynamic application.

Kooboo’s site log records changes across CMS stores and dynamic-table data. History APIs can list recent changes, find the versions of a particular object, retrieve a log item, and compare two recorded versions of the same object.

This applies to the things that actually make the application work:

  • Pages, layouts, and views
  • Styles, scripts, code, and routes
  • Images and website files
  • Labels, forms, menus, and HTML blocks
  • Content structures and content records
  • Supported dynamic-table records
  • Other versioned Kooboo site objects

A developer can examine what changed without reducing the application to a page-level timestamp.

Recover at the right scale

Different mistakes need different recovery tools. Kooboo supports several levels.

Undo one change

Select a history item and undo it. Kooboo applies the inverse operation and records the recovery as new history.

Undo a selected set of changes

Several validated log items can be undone together. The current service validates the requested IDs before it begins the rollback operation and places a safety limit on the number accepted in one request.

Restore the website to a log position

Kooboo can roll back later recorded changes until the website returns to the state represented by a selected log ID.

Restore by time

The site can be restored to the last recorded state at or before a specified date and time.

Check out history as another website

Sometimes the safest recovery is not to touch the current website at all. Kooboo can create another website containing the source site’s state at a chosen history log. The historical site can receive its own name and domain and can remain unpublished while it is inspected.

Do not guess what the old website looked like. Open it as a website.

Restore and checkout operations have explicit processing limits in the current implementation. These limits protect the server from unbounded rollback work and should be included in administrator documentation.

AI can use the same history—with approval boundaries

Kooboo exposes structured AI functions for history operations. AI can list history, inspect items, list versions, compare versions, undo selected changes, restore to a log or time, and check out a historical state as another site.

Operations that change state require approval. This is an important distinction between an AI that merely writes code and an AI operating a production platform.

An effective AI workflow can become:

  1. Inspect the current object and relevant history.
  2. Explain the difference.
  3. Request approval for the recovery operation.
  4. Apply the change.
  5. Open or request the affected URL and verify the result.

History gives AI a factual record of the application instead of asking it to reconstruct the previous state from conversation alone.

A Sandbox is a real Kooboo website

Kooboo’s AI Sandbox creates a separate hidden website inside the organization. It runs through the same Kooboo website model and runtime as the original site.

That matters because many staging environments fail in subtle ways: different framework versions, missing services, different routes, different database assumptions, or deployment-only behavior. Kooboo reduces that class of difference by testing the work as another Kooboo site rather than inventing a separate simulation runtime.

The current Sandbox functions can:

  • Create and delete a hidden Sandbox site
  • List Sandboxes in the organization
  • Copy selected supported object types from the current site
  • Run KScript in the Sandbox context
  • Evaluate a <k-data> block
  • Render a template
  • Request and render a Sandbox page while measuring execution time
  • Use normal AI editing functions against the selected Sandbox

AI can therefore change an isolated copy, inspect the code, execute server logic, render pages, and use browser control to test the result before the production website is changed.

The testing runtime and production runtime are the same kind of system

Containers became essential partly because development and production environments drift. Kooboo approaches the problem at the application-platform level.

A Kooboo site carries its pages, layouts, views, styles, scripts, routes, content definitions, data, and platform objects. A Sandbox, local instance, hosted instance, and remote Kooboo server use the same application model and universal runtime.

This does not mean operating systems, networks, permissions, domains, or external integrations can never differ. It means the website is not rebuilt from several unrelated framework projects merely to reach another Kooboo environment.

Move the whole application—or the part you need

Kooboo provides more than one movement model because deployment and distribution are not always the same task.

Complete website packages

A full Kooboo website can be exported to a portable package and imported as another site. The package can include application objects, dynamic tables, file storage, commerce data, module files, and supported site settings.

Selected object categories

Kooboo can export selected stores instead of the entire website. The current export path adds several known companion stores—for example form settings with forms and authorization data with OpenAPI objects.

Selected history batches

Change-log items can be packaged as a batch and imported into another Kooboo site. This provides a deployment unit based on recorded changes rather than copying an entire database every time.

Remote incremental publish

Kooboo remote publishing reads website changes from the sync log and sends them to another Kooboo server in bounded batches. After the initial connection, later pushes can transfer new application changes rather than reinstalling the complete website.

The same service supports pulling remote changes back into the current site.

Conflicts are information—not permission to overwrite

If both local and remote sites have changed the same object, Kooboo’s synchronization service checks for a conflict. A push or pull can stop and return information about the local and remote versions, users, modification times, object bodies, and image status where applicable.

This is safer than treating deployment as blind file replacement. The user can see that the destination has meaningful work before choosing how to proceed.

Remote publish destinations can also define object stores to ignore for outgoing or incoming synchronization. That allows an administrator to keep environment-specific categories out of a particular direction of transfer.

Deployment is efficient because it follows the edit log

A production deployment does not always require scanning and serializing the full website. Kooboo’s remote publisher asks the sync log for pending items, prepares the corresponding typed object, sends it to the remote receiver, and records the acknowledged remote version.

This favors incremental work:

  • Transfer the changes that have not yet been published.
  • Process them in bounded batches.
  • Stop cleanly when finished, when the batch limit is reached, or when a conflict appears.
  • Continue later from the recorded synchronization state.

The current implementation uses source-generated JSON metadata for key publishing, synchronization, history, and AI contracts. That supports Kooboo’s NativeAOT direction and avoids making reflection-based serialization a deployment requirement.

What still needs to be completed: Sandbox promotion

The Sandbox is already useful for isolated AI development and testing. Copying selected object types into a Sandbox is also implemented.

However, the final Sandbox-to-production promotion workflow should not yet be marketed as a complete atomic deployment system.

The high-value next step is a dependency-aware change set that can:

  • Compare the complete Sandbox change set with production
  • Include the required dependent objects
  • Show additions, updates, and deletions before approval
  • Run persistent acceptance tests against the proposed result
  • Promote the approved change set as one controlled operation
  • Roll back the promotion if verification fails
  • Expire and clean up abandoned Sandboxes according to policy

Kooboo already has important building blocks: typed site objects, relation data, edit logs, object comparison, packages, remote synchronization, hidden Sandboxes, AI functions, and browser testing. Completing promotion will connect them into a particularly strong AI delivery pipeline.

History is not a backup strategy by itself

Application history protects against many editing mistakes, but it should not replace independent operational backups. Hardware failure, storage corruption, administrator error, credential compromise, and infrastructure loss require copies outside the active server.

A responsible Kooboo production setup should combine:

  • Object and site history for fast operational recovery
  • Portable exports for application movement and archival
  • Remote publication for controlled delivery
  • Independent server and data backups
  • Release verification and recovery testing

The strength is not a magical “undo everything” promise. It is the number of useful recovery and movement choices available before a problem becomes a disaster.

One lifecycle for human and AI development

Kooboo brings the application lifecycle into one understandable sequence:

Edit → Record → Compare → Test → Approve → Package or Publish → Verify → Undo or Restore when necessary

Humans can use that lifecycle from the administration interface, inline editor, IDE, CLI, packages, and remote publishing tools. AI can use structured functions against the same website objects, history, Sandbox, and runtime.

The fastest development platform is not the one that never makes a mistake. It is the one that makes every change visible, testable, movable, and recoverable.

Kooboo History & Deployment: Move quickly because the platform remembers how to come back.

Kooboo Relation Intelligence

A Website That Understands Itself

See what site objects use, where they are used, and what a change will affect.

A modern website is not a folder of independent files.

A page depends on a layout. The layout loads styles and scripts. A view queries content. CSS refers to images and fonts. Links point to routes. Components contain other components. The same image may appear in a page, a product, a style rule, and an email.

Most development tools store these pieces, but they do not understand the complete website relationship. When something moves or disappears, developers discover the consequences later: a broken image, an old URL, a missing dependency, stale browser content, or a component that looked unused but was not.

Kooboo treats these connections as part of the website itself.

The website is not only its objects. It is also the relationships between those objects.

Demo one: find every place an image is used

Open an image in Kooboo and inspect its relationships. Instead of searching through source files and hoping every reference has the same spelling, Kooboo can show the website objects that use it.

  1. Select an image used in several areas of the website.
  2. Open its relation or “used by” information.
  3. Show the pages, layouts, views, styles, or other objects that refer to it.
  4. Open one of those consumers directly.
  5. Replace or edit the image and verify the affected pages.

The same relationship model is useful for more than images. Kooboo records typed connections between many site objects, including pages, layouts, views, styles, scripts, resource groups, routes, labels, HTML blocks, forms, components, content, files, and external resources.

Demo two: change a URL without leaving old references behind

URL changes are deceptively expensive. A route may be referenced by navigation, content, HTML attributes, layouts, views, styles, or other application objects.

In Kooboo, route relationships identify the objects that refer to a URL. When the route is updated through the supported URL-editing workflow, Kooboo can update those known consumers and rebuild the corresponding relationships.

  1. Create a page at /old-product.
  2. Link to it from a page, layout, and reusable view.
  3. Rename the route to /new-product.
  4. Open each consumer and show the updated reference.
  5. Run link diagnosis and confirm that the old internal link is no longer used.

Relation intelligence begins when the source is saved

Kooboo has its own HTML DOM engine. When a source-aware website object is added or changed, Kooboo can parse the real document structure and compute relationships from it.

The relation engine recognizes connections such as:

  • Referenced stylesheets and scripts
  • Images and website files
  • Internal links and external URLs
  • Layouts used by pages
  • Components embedded in other objects
  • Inline styles and CSS class use
  • Labels, HTML blocks, forms, and configuration objects
  • Embedded styles, scripts, forms, and KScript blocks
  • Video and other routed resources

Each relationship retains the identity and type of both sides. Kooboo therefore knows more than “this text appears somewhere.” It knows that a Page refers to a Route whose destination is an Image, or that a View is used by a Page.

This is a practical object graph built into the site database.

Ask both questions: “What does this use?” and “What uses this?”

A relationship becomes useful only when it can be followed in both directions.

From a page, Kooboo can inspect the layouts, views, resources, components, and routes it uses. From an image, style, view, or route, Kooboo can inspect the objects that use it.

That changes common maintenance work:

  • Before editing: understand the scope of the change.
  • Before deleting: inspect the consumers that may be affected.
  • After importing: identify missing or external resources.
  • During debugging: move from a rendered problem to the responsible object.
  • During optimization: find large images and the pages that use them.
  • During packaging: understand which objects belong together.

Kooboo does not need to rediscover the entire application through text search every time a user asks one of these questions.

External resources become visible—and can become local

External resources are easy to add and easy to forget. A template may depend on a remote font, image, stylesheet, or script. That dependency can affect privacy, performance, reliability, security policy, and long-term ownership.

Kooboo records recognized external URLs as external-resource objects and connects them to the source objects that use them. Users and AI can list those URLs instead of treating them as invisible strings scattered through the website.

Kooboo can then internalize supported external images, scripts, and styles:

  1. Download the resource into the Kooboo website.
  2. Create the corresponding local object and route.
  3. For a stylesheet, inspect and download supported referenced resources recursively.
  4. Use the relation map to replace known consumers with the new local URL.

This is particularly valuable when making third-party assets—such as externally hosted fonts—part of the site that the owner controls. It can reduce runtime dependence on another host and can help with privacy and availability, although licensing terms must still permit local hosting.

If the website depends on it, Kooboo should be able to show it.

Diagnosis becomes specific instead of generic

A scan that reports “missing image” is useful. A scan that also reports where the missing image is used is actionable.

Kooboo’s diagnosis and automation code combines resource checks with relation data. It can identify conditions such as:

  • Internal links whose destination is missing
  • Missing images
  • External links that should be validated
  • Images above configured size expectations
  • Malformed HTML and duplicate element IDs

For relationship-aware checks, the report can include the objects that use the problem resource. The developer can move from symptom to source without manually crawling the website.

Cache versioning follows the object version

Long browser caching improves performance, but it creates a familiar deployment problem: the browser may keep an old image, stylesheet, or script after the website changes.

Kooboo can append a version query parameter to eligible local asset URLs. The value comes from the current website object or route version. When a versioned image, style, script, resource group, or supported module resource changes, its rendered URL can change as well.

That creates a simple performance contract:

  • An unchanged asset can remain cached.
  • A changed asset receives a changed URL.
  • The browser requests the new version instead of reusing stale content.

The developer does not need to rename every file manually or run a separate fingerprinting pipeline for ordinary Kooboo-managed resources.

The inline editor works because Kooboo understands the source

Relation intelligence and source-aware editing reinforce each other.

The inline editor can connect a rendered element back to the page, layout, view, content, style, or other source that produced it. The relation system adds another dimension: how that source participates in the rest of the website.

A user can begin with what is visible, trace it to the responsible source, and then inspect the objects connected to that source. This is much closer to editing a living application than editing a screenshot of one.

AI needs structure, not a larger text search

An AI that sees only files must infer the architecture from names and text. That works until names are ambiguous, content is generated dynamically, or a URL is referenced through several object types.

Kooboo can give AI structured operations for listing external URLs, internalizing selected resources, reading object context, inspecting rendered elements, and changing routes. The platform’s object and relation model provides safer context for those operations.

This does not make every generated reference automatically knowable. A URL assembled dynamically at runtime may not be visible to static relation analysis. Custom code and unusual source formats still require testing. The advantage is that ordinary website relationships are first-class platform data rather than undocumented developer knowledge.

Designed for runtime use, not a heavyweight graph service

Kooboo stores relation records in its own site database and represents object types with compact identifiers. Relationship lookup is part of the same local application model as pages, routes, content, and resources.

This matters for a high-density Web OS. Relation intelligence should not require a separate search cluster or graph server for every website. It should remain available to the editor, diagnosis engine, deployment tools, KScript, and AI without turning ordinary page rendering into a network of external services.

The relation model and its supporting objects use explicit serialization paths in the Kooboo codebase, fitting the platform’s NativeAOT direction without making runtime reflection the foundation of the feature.

What relation intelligence does—and does not—promise

Kooboo can understand relationships that its parsers, repositories, routes, and supported object formats recognize. It can use those relationships for navigation, diagnosis, reference updates, localization, and cache behavior.

It should not be described as infallible static analysis of arbitrary JavaScript. A URL constructed from several runtime values, fetched from an unknown external API, or hidden inside an unsupported custom format may not appear in the relation map.

The correct promise is more useful:

Kooboo turns the normal structure of a website into actionable platform knowledge.

That knowledge reduces accidental breakage, makes maintenance faster, gives AI better context, and helps the owner keep the application understandable as it grows.

Kooboo Relation Intelligence: Change the website with an understanding of what the change touches.

Kooboo Server-Side Analytics

Measure What Really Happened

Measure at the server. Understand the journey. Keep the data yours.

Most website analytics begins by adding another company’s JavaScript to every page.

The browser downloads the tracker, executes it, creates or reads identifiers, sends visitor data to another system, and reports what it was able to observe. The website owner then tries to reconnect those reports with the website, the application, the customer database, the commerce system, the consent platform, and the real business outcome.

Kooboo starts from the opposite side.

The website is already running inside Kooboo. The server already receives the request, resolves the route, renders the page, executes the API, knows the response status, measures the execution time, and writes the response. Kooboo can record that first-party operational event directly—without requiring a general-purpose analytics library in the visitor’s browser.

The server does not need to ask the browser whether the server received a request.

This simple architectural decision changes much more than page-view counting. It improves performance, reduces third-party data flows, connects analytics with real website objects and backend events, and makes the resulting data available to developers and AI inside the same platform.

Proof one: remove the analytics script and keep the analytics

We will provide a small Kooboo website package for a direct test.

  1. Download and import the website into a Kooboo instance.
  2. Open the site in a private browser window.
  3. Inspect the page source and the Network panel.
  4. Confirm that the page does not load Google Analytics, Google Tag Manager, or another browser analytics library.
  5. Visit several pages, including one missing URL.
  6. Open Kooboo Analytics and inspect the recorded page views, routes, referrers, response statuses, execution times, devices, countries, and error page.

Download the Kooboo Server-Side Analytics demo

The result is not a browser estimate of whether the page might have loaded. It is a record created from the request and response path that actually ran.

Proof two: record the business result where it becomes real

A conversion should represent a business outcome, not merely a browser reaching a URL.

A visitor may load a thank-you page twice. A payment can be declined after the browser event. A webhook can confirm payment when the customer has already closed the tab. An order can be created by an API, an administrator, an automated process, or another application. Browser-only tracking sees only the part that happens in the browser.

Kooboo’s analytics architecture can receive goals from the website itself:

  • A Page is rendered.
  • An API or server Code route executes.
  • A commerce event occurs, such as an order being created or paid.
  • Server-side KScript records a configured custom business event.
  • An optional first-party interaction tracker records a configured click for page-interaction reporting.

For example:

<script env="server">
  // Record an event from the server-side application flow.
  k.analytics.track("qualified_lead");
</script>

The script executes on the Kooboo server. It is not delivered to the visitor’s browser. The event can participate in the same navigation and goal model as the surrounding website.

The second demonstration will show a visitor entering the website, moving through product pages, creating an order, and completing a backend commerce event. The report will then show the path and its business outcome without depending on an external conversion pixel.

Analytics should describe the website—not add another system beside it

Conventional analytics is often separated from the application it measures. It knows URLs, events, and browser identifiers, but it may not know which Kooboo Page produced the response, which server route executed, which commerce state existed, which resource failed, or which backend event made the conversion real.

Kooboo records analytics inside a platform that already understands the website. The current request capture can include:

  • The requested URL, host, referrer, and same-site request context
  • The Kooboo Page or website object associated with the route
  • The response status, response size, and server execution time
  • UTM campaign information
  • Browser, device, mobile state, and User-Agent information
  • Country, city, continent, network organization, and connection classification derived on the server
  • Available Client Hints such as viewport width, device-pixel ratio, color preference, connection type, round-trip time, and downlink
  • Bot classification and whether the request came from human or automated traffic
  • Existing customer, cart, session, and consent context when applicable

Not every browser sends every hint, and Kooboo should not invent missing information. Reports use the information available on the real request.

The current dashboard can summarize page views, unique visitors, daily trends, top pages, referrers, countries, browsers, devices, viewport widths, color schemes, connection characteristics, error pages, and human-versus-bot traffic.

One request can explain traffic, performance, errors, resources, navigation, and business context because those facts belong to the same runtime.

No analytics JavaScript on the critical path

A browser analytics library has a cost even when it loads asynchronously. It adds another request, more JavaScript to download and parse, more work on the main thread, another network endpoint, and another component that can fail or be blocked.

Kooboo’s normal visitor analytics does not need that library. Request capture runs from Kooboo’s render-completion pipeline. The page can finish rendering and return its own content without waiting for a third-party analytics service.

The implementation is designed to keep heavier analytics work away from the response path:

  1. Kooboo captures a compact work item when rendering completes.
  2. Typed concurrent queues separate visitor, resource, error, site-error, and code-event work.
  3. A background worker enriches, groups, stores, and aggregates those records.
  4. Generated binary records and Kooboo’s IndexedDB storage avoid turning every analytics event into a large general-purpose object document.
  5. Daily B-tree, B+tree, WORM, and memory-mapped stores support bounded reporting and flow analysis.

The analytics APIs also impose practical query boundaries. Current KScript analytics queries limit date ranges, page sizes, and top-value counts so that application code cannot casually request unbounded reports.

This is an architecture for production measurement, not a script pasted into a page after the website has already been designed.

Privacy-first does not mean pretending that data is anonymous

Server-side analytics removes the need to send every measurement to a third-party analytics provider, but server-side processing can still involve personal data. IP addresses, customer identifiers, request metadata, and linkable behavioral records require a real privacy design.

Kooboo’s current identity logic uses several levels of context:

  1. When a known commerce customer exists, Kooboo uses a salted hash of that customer identity for analytics correlation.
  2. When analytics consent allows it and an existing session identifier is available, Kooboo hashes that session identifier.
  3. Otherwise, Kooboo derives a pseudonymous daily identifier from request metadata, including the IP address and browser request headers, using a site-specific daily salt.

Kooboo uses the IP address to derive location and network information, then anonymizes the raw IP field stored in the visitor record. The daily salt limits long-term linkage of the fallback identifier while allowing same-day navigation analysis.

This is pseudonymization, not a promise of complete anonymity. Under GDPR, pseudonymized information can remain personal data. The website operator still needs an appropriate lawful basis, clear information, purpose limitation, data minimization, retention rules, security, and a process for applicable data-subject rights.

The ePrivacy question is related but different. A system that does not store or access information on the visitor’s device may avoid the specific device-storage mechanism that causes many analytics cookie banners, depending on the exact implementation and applicable national law. That does not automatically remove GDPR obligations for server-side processing.

Kooboo reduces unnecessary third-party collection. It does not replace the organization’s legal decisions with a marketing slogan.

For many websites, built-in analytics removes the reason for an analytics cookie banner

Many websites add a consent banner primarily because they have added a third-party analytics product that writes identifiers in the browser or accesses device information for tracking.

If a Kooboo website uses only its built-in request analytics, does not enable optional browser interaction tracking, does not use another browser identifier, and does not load unrelated tracking services, the technical architecture is much simpler:

Visitor → your Kooboo website → analytics stored in your chosen Kooboo environment

There is no separate analytics SaaS in that path and no general-purpose analytics script to execute in the browser. For many ordinary websites, that can remove the technical reason they introduced an analytics cookie banner in the first place.

Whether consent is legally required still depends on what the site processes, the operator’s purpose and lawful basis, the visitor’s jurisdiction, and any additional technologies on the page. A legal conclusion must be based on the actual deployment, not merely the product name.

The practical advantage is important: Kooboo lets the website owner begin with first-party server measurement and add consent-requiring technology only when the website genuinely needs it.

When consent is needed, Kooboo enforces it before the resource loads

A real website may still need an advertising network, embedded video, external analytics tool, marketing pixel, chat widget, or another optional resource. In that case, a banner alone is not enough. The site must prevent the resource from loading before the applicable choice.

Kooboo’s consent system is integrated with server-side HTML rendering. The website owner can associate external resource URL patterns with consent categories. When Kooboo renders a configured <script>, <img>, <iframe>, or <link>, the renderer checks the visitor’s consent state before producing the loading attribute.

If the category is not allowed, Kooboo changes the real loading attribute:

<!-- Original website source -->
<script src="https://tracker.example/analytics.js"></script>

<!-- Rendered before analytics consent -->
<script kc-src="https://tracker.example/analytics.js"
        kc-category="analytics"></script>

Because the browser does not receive a src attribute for that script, it does not request the blocked JavaScript file. For a blocked iframe, Kooboo can render a first-party fallback page instead of loading the external frame. When the visitor later allows the category, the first-party consent client restores the resource and executes it.

This is stronger than loading a tracker and asking it not to collect data. The optional resource is prevented from loading at the HTML attribute level before the browser makes the request.

The current implementation covers the primary src and href cases for scripts, images, iframes, and links. Additional URL-bearing elements and attributes should be included before claiming universal resource coverage.

See the path, not only the total

A page-view chart says how much traffic arrived. It does not explain what people did next.

Kooboo’s navigation-flow engine turns website requests into nodes and transitions. A same-site referrer or the visitor’s previous known node can connect one request to the next. Daily unique stores distinguish repeated activity from unique users and unique transitions, while flow statistics retain visit counts, transitions, drop-off, and goals associated with the originating node.

A flow can begin with manually selected steps or with an automatically suggested path built from popular transitions. Reports can then answer questions such as:

  • Where do visitors enter?
  • Which page do they visit next?
  • Which paths reach a goal?
  • Where do people leave?
  • Which entry page produces useful outcomes rather than empty traffic?
  • How do logged-in customer journeys differ from anonymous same-day journeys?

Kooboo does not need to export page events to one platform, orders to another platform, and customer state to a third before attempting to reconstruct the journey. Those events can meet inside the website runtime.

Fallback same-day correlation is probabilistic because different visitors can share request characteristics and one visitor’s characteristics can change. Reports should present it as pseudonymous journey analysis, not as a guaranteed real-world identity.

A goal can be a page, an API, a business event, or your own code

Different websites define success differently. A publisher may value a subscription. A manufacturer may value a qualified enquiry. An ecommerce site may value a paid order. A support application may value a resolved case.

Kooboo’s goal model is designed around the source of the real outcome:

  • Page goal: a specific Kooboo Page is reached.
  • API goal: a server Code or API route executes.
  • Commerce goal: a system event such as cart creation, product viewing, customer creation, order creation, payment, or shipment occurs.
  • Custom goal: application logic calls k.analytics.track(...) for a configured event name.

This reduces the pressure to force every business outcome into a browser event. The developer can record the goal where the application actually knows it happened.

Click tracking is deliberately separate from normal server request analytics. When page interaction tracking is enabled, Kooboo adds a small first-party script that listens only to configured k-track elements and sends the selected event back to the same Kooboo site. Sites that do not need click-level interaction data can leave it disabled. The current implementation records these page interactions separately; they should not be presented as selectable conversion goals until that workflow is completed and tested.

Analytics includes errors, resources, bandwidth, and bots

Traffic is only one part of understanding a live website.

Because Kooboo observes the running request and website object model, the same analytics foundation also supports operational questions.

Error monitoring

Kooboo records page, API, and custom code errors and can summarize trends, status codes, affected users, and high-frequency failures. Missing page requests also appear in visitor reporting, while suspicious path-scanning requests can feed Kooboo’s IP protection logic.

Resource Guardian

Resource reports can show human and bot requests, bandwidth, file types, missing resources, source pages, external domains, protected resources, and the pages that reference a resource. This helps answer practical questions:

  • Which image or file consumes the most bandwidth?
  • Which page is requesting a missing resource?
  • How much resource traffic comes from bots?
  • Which external domains are involved in the website?
  • Which resources are being requested from unexpected sources?

Bot analysis

Kooboo separates human visits from detected bots, classifies known automated traffic, reports its traffic share, and can show whether a bot is allowed or blocked. A sudden traffic increase can therefore be understood as human demand, useful search crawling, or unwanted automation instead of appearing as one undifferentiated number.

Analytics should help operate the website, not merely prepare a monthly traffic slide.

Your analytics is programmable

A fixed dashboard can answer only the questions its designer predicted.

Kooboo exposes visitor, resource, and error analytics to server-side KScript. A developer can build a private dashboard, place selected metrics in an administration application, trigger a workflow, or combine analytics with the website’s own business data.

<script env="server">
  const traffic = k.analytics.visitor.summary({
    startDate: "2026-08-01",
    endDate: "2026-08-10",
    top: 20,
    includeDimensions: true
  });

  const errors = k.analytics.error.summary({
    startDate: "2026-08-01",
    endDate: "2026-08-10",
    top: 10
  });
</script>

Detail and summary APIs are available for:

  • k.analytics.visitor.list(...) and k.analytics.visitor.summary(...)
  • k.analytics.resource.list(...) and k.analytics.resource.summary(...)
  • k.analytics.error.list(...) and k.analytics.error.summary(...)
  • k.analytics.track(...) for custom application events

The public query surface uses bounded date ranges, pagination, and top-value limits. Resource detail comes from a bounded recent-resource store, while resource summaries use the complete aggregated data for the selected range.

Kooboo’s analytics KScript types include explicit NativeAOT preservation annotations, and analytics JSON paths use source-generated metadata where configured. That keeps the programmable surface aligned with Kooboo’s high-performance, AOT-compatible runtime direction.

AI can investigate the live website with the same data

Kooboo’s native AI does not have to ask the user to copy numbers from an external dashboard. Built-in AI functions can read visitor overviews and logs, Resource Guardian reports and logs, and error-monitoring reports and logs for the current website.

This makes questions such as these possible:

  • Which pages received the most human traffic this week?
  • Which missing resources affect the most requests?
  • Did a release increase page or API errors?
  • Which countries experience the highest reported round-trip time?
  • How much traffic came from bots?
  • Which external resource domains are used most heavily?

Because AI can also inspect website source, Pages, routes, rendered output, and browser behavior, analytics can become the beginning of an investigation rather than the end of a report.

The long-term operating loop is straightforward:

Observe → explain → locate the responsible website object → change safely → test → compare the result

One first-party system instead of an analytics integration project

Kooboo Server-Side Analytics is not valuable because it reproduces every chart from a standalone analytics product. It is valuable because it removes boundaries that should never have existed.

  • The analytics recorder is not separated from the web server.
  • The route is not separated from the Page or API that produced it.
  • The navigation flow is not separated from backend business events.
  • The error report is not separated from the source objects AI and developers can inspect.
  • The resource report is not separated from bandwidth, missing files, external domains, and bot traffic.
  • The analytics data is not limited to a fixed dashboard; KScript and AI can query it.
  • The website owner does not have to export every visitor event to a separate analytics SaaS.
  • The browser does not need to download a general-purpose analytics library for normal request measurement.

For a simple website, that can mean useful analytics without adding a third-party tracker or an analytics-driven cookie banner. For a dynamic application, it can mean connecting navigation to the backend event that represents real value. For an operations team, it can mean seeing traffic, errors, resources, bots, and performance in one runtime. For AI, it provides the evidence needed to improve the website it operates.

Do not add analytics to the website. Build the website on a platform that already understands what happened.

What we are completing next

Kooboo’s request analytics, reporting, resource monitoring, error monitoring, programmable analytics, AI access, navigation flow, and multiple goal sources already exist in the current platform. The next work is focused on making outcome measurement more explicit and auditable:

  • Apply configured goal deduplication by business entity or time window.
  • Show the evidence used to attribute and reconcile a business outcome.
  • Connect verified goal conversions consistently to server-side A/B test reporting.
  • Add clearer privacy modes, minimization controls, retention controls, and deployment guidance.
  • Benchmark and publish the measured overhead of analytics under production concurrency.
  • Expand consent-resource coverage beyond the primary script, image, iframe, and link attributes.

We are publishing the architecture now because the direction matters: analytics should be first-party, server-aware, programmable, privacy-conscious, and connected to real application outcomes. As the remaining workflow is completed, the demonstrations in this article will be updated with downloadable sites, screenshots, benchmark results, and repeatable test instructions.

Legal and technical references

  • General Data Protection Regulation
  • ePrivacy Directive, especially Article 5(3)
  • EDPB Guidelines 2/2023 on the technical scope of Article 5(3)
  • European Commission guidance on lawful processing conditions

Kooboo Server-Side Analytics: Real requests. Real outcomes. First-party control.

Description_en: Your Domain, Website, and Business Email—Ready Together
Body_en:
Kooboo Domain & Email

Your Domain, Website, and Business Email—Ready Together

One account. Multiple domains. Every inbox. No infrastructure puzzle.

Creating a website has become easier. Connecting that website to the internet has not.

A business owner chooses a domain, then meets nameservers, DNS zones, A records, CNAME records, certificate challenges, MX priorities, SPF policies, DKIM selectors, DMARC alignment, SMTP settings, and mailbox administration. Every item is manageable for an experienced administrator. Together, they create a fragile technical project for someone who simply wants a secure website and a professional email address.

Kooboo removes that boundary.

Choose the domain. Create the website. Create the email address. Kooboo connects the infrastructure.

Kooboo combines website hosting with its own domain, DNS, SSL, and mail infrastructure. A domain registered through Kooboo can move directly into website and email use. An existing domain can use Kooboo DNS after its nameservers are delegated once. From that point, Kooboo can coordinate the records required by the website and mail system.

Demo one: from a domain to a secure website

The first demonstration should begin with an account that has no website.

  1. Register a new domain through Kooboo, or select a domain already connected to Kooboo DNS.
  2. Create a Kooboo website and assign the domain.
  3. Open the domain in a browser.
  4. Confirm that the website resolves correctly and HTTPS is active.
  5. Open the domain settings and show the DNS records Kooboo manages.

The user does not need to copy a certificate to the server, configure a reverse proxy, schedule certificate renewal, or manually connect a hostname to the correct Kooboo site.

Demo two: create business email on the same domain

Continue with the same domain:

  1. Create hello@example.com.
  2. Open the Kooboo inbox.
  3. Send a message to an external mail provider.
  4. Reply to the message and receive it in Kooboo.
  5. Show the MX, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration associated with the domain.

This is the complete outcome a business understands:

Website: https://example.com
Email: hello@example.com

The protocols remain real internet standards. Kooboo simply manages their relationship for the user.

DNS should be infrastructure—not homework

DNS translates the names people use into the services computers need. It is foundational, but most website owners should not need to manage it record by record.

Kooboo operates its own authoritative DNS system. Its central account system holds the domain configuration, while Kooboo DNS servers maintain a local cache with a default twelve-hour lifetime. This provides a centrally managed domain model without requiring every lookup to depend on a live account-service request.

Because Kooboo understands its own website and mail services, it can coordinate records for:

  • Root domains and subdomains
  • Website bindings
  • Mail delivery
  • Sender authentication
  • Service verification

A user can still inspect and manage DNS when necessary. The difference is that ordinary Kooboo workflows do not begin by asking the user to become a DNS administrator.

HTTPS is created when the website needs it

Kooboo’s runtime selects certificates according to the requested hostname. When a valid certificate is not already available for an eligible bound domain, Kooboo can request certificate generation on demand through its SSL service.

The certificate service uses Let’s Encrypt. Kooboo stores the resulting certificate for the domain, caches it for request handling, and runs a background renewal process. Certificates approaching expiry are renewed automatically, and request-time certificate selection can also trigger renewal before the certificate becomes invalid.

The website owner experiences the result rather than the certificate lifecycle:

Bind the domain → open the website securely → Kooboo maintains the certificate

Certificate issuance still depends on successful domain validation and the availability and policies of the certificate authority. Kooboo automates the workflow; it cannot override public DNS or certificate-authority requirements.

Email authentication belongs with the domain

Receiving mail requires MX records. Responsible sending also requires domain-authentication policy.

  • SPF tells receiving systems which servers are authorized to send for the domain.
  • DKIM signs outgoing messages so recipients can verify the sending domain and message integrity.
  • DMARC defines alignment and handling policy and creates a reporting channel for authentication results.

Kooboo’s mail system contains SPF validation, DKIM handling, and DMARC report processing. The mail interface exposes domain security reporting, and the DNS/account integration can prepare the domain records required by the Kooboo mail service.

Correct records are essential, but they do not guarantee inbox placement. Sending reputation, message quality, complaint rates, volume patterns, recipient engagement, and the reputation of the sending infrastructure still affect delivery.

One person is not the same thing as one inbox

Traditional email hosting often begins with a rigid assumption:

One account → one mailbox

Real organizations are more complicated. One person may operate several brands, domains, roles, and public addresses. The same user may need:

  • guoqi@example.com
  • support@example.com
  • sales@another-brand.com
  • A catch-all address for a domain
  • A forwarding address
  • A group address shared with several people

Kooboo models the user and organization separately from the addresses. One user can own multiple email addresses across the organization’s domains. The current address model supports:

  • Normal addresses for ordinary sending and receiving
  • Forwarding addresses that deliver to another destination
  • Group addresses with multiple members
  • Wildcard addresses that can receive matching addresses dynamically

Messages are stored in a user-level mail database with address identity attached to each message. The web interface can show combined folders or filter by address. A user can choose the appropriate From address when composing or replying.

The inbox belongs to the user. The addresses describe the roles through which that user communicates.

Kooboo adapts IMAP to the multi-address model

Users may prefer a familiar desktop or mobile mail client. Kooboo therefore provides IMAP with TLS support and common operations such as listing folders, selecting mailboxes, searching, fetching, copying, moving, appending, and updating flags.

The folder model adapts standard IMAP presentation to Kooboo’s account design. When a user has several addresses, Kooboo can expose address-specific folders below the inbox while keeping the normal Sent, Drafts, Spam, and Trash structure.

That allows an ordinary mail client to navigate a model that is richer than one account with one address.

Mail is more than an inbox

The current Kooboo mail application also includes capabilities such as:

  • Folders and subscriptions
  • Advanced search
  • Contacts
  • Per-address signatures
  • Default sender selection
  • Attachments
  • Calendar invitations and replies
  • Migration from another IMAP mailbox
  • SMTP configuration
  • DMARC reports
  • BIMI and Verified Mark Certificate configuration

Kooboo also connects business email with the website’s other communication systems: transactional messages from applications, commerce notifications, and integrated email marketing.

An existing domain needs one honest first step

If a domain is registered through Kooboo, Kooboo can manage the relationship from registration onward.

If the domain is registered elsewhere, the registrar still controls its nameserver delegation. The owner must point the domain to Kooboo DNS once. After that delegation has propagated, Kooboo can manage the website and mail records inside its own system.

This distinction should be stated clearly. Kooboo removes record-by-record configuration after the domain is under Kooboo DNS; it cannot change an external registrar’s nameserver settings without authorization.

Why this belongs in a Web OS

A page builder can stop after publishing HTML. A Web OS must help the application become a real, secure, reachable service.

Kooboo connects:

  • The organization to its domains
  • The domain to its DNS zone
  • The hostname to the correct website
  • The website to an automatically maintained certificate
  • The mail domain to its delivery and authentication records
  • The user to multiple addresses and inbox views
  • The business application to transactional and marketing communication

The user no longer assembles a registrar, DNS provider, certificate tool, hosting panel, mailbox provider, and marketing platform before the business can communicate.

Your domain should identify the whole business—not begin another infrastructure project.

Kooboo Domain & Email: One account for every domain, website, and business conversation.

Description_en: Email Marketing That Runs Like a Website
Body_en:
Kooboo Email Marketing

Email Marketing That Runs Like a Website

Write it like a web page. Render it for one person. Know exactly what was sent.

Most email platforms begin by asking you to export or synchronize your customer data. You create a list in one system, build a template in another, connect the two with an integration, and hope that every field, consent state, purchase, and unsubscribe remains synchronized.

Kooboo begins with a different question:

If the website already contains the customer, content, products, orders, business logic, and rendering engine, why should email marketing live somewhere else?

Email marketing is built directly into Kooboo. A campaign can use the website's own data, server-side JavaScript, rendering system, automation, tracking, and delivery records. The same platform that runs the website can generate a different email for every recipient.

This is more than adding merge fields to a newsletter. A Kooboo campaign can behave like a server-rendered email application.

The privacy problem begins when email leaves the website

A conventional email-marketing setup is not only a technical integration. It creates another data-processing relationship.

The website collects names, email addresses, consent records, customer attributes, purchases, and behavior. That data is then copied or synchronized to an external marketing platform. The external platform may engage its own subprocessors, operate infrastructure in several countries, add an open-tracking image, and route clicks through its own servers.

For an organization serving people in Europe, each additional step can create work:

  • Identify the external provider as a processor and put the required processing agreement in place.
  • Review the provider's subprocessors and the data each one receives.
  • Determine where customer data and tracking events are processed.
  • Assess transfers to countries outside the European Economic Area and the applicable transfer mechanism.
  • Explain the processing, tracking, recipients, retention, and rights clearly to the customer.
  • Keep website consent, newsletter consent, unsubscribes, and vendor-side tracking preferences synchronized.

This is not theoretical. GDPR Article 28 requires a controller using a processor to choose a processor providing sufficient guarantees and to govern the processing by contract. GDPR Chapter V applies when personal data is transferred to a third country. Such transfers are not automatically prohibited, but the controller must establish an appropriate legal mechanism, such as an adequacy decision or suitable safeguards.

Mailchimp provides a familiar example of this model. Its own Data Processing Addendum says that it processes customer data as a processor, may engage subprocessors, and may process data in the United States and elsewhere, subject to the applicable transfer safeguards.

The problem is not that an external platform can never be compliant. The problem is that every external platform adds another organization, contract, data flow, tracking endpoint, and compliance dependency.

A website cookie choice does not automatically cover email tracking

A visitor may accept or reject optional tracking on a website. Later, the same person receives an email generated and tracked by another platform. The website's consent record does not automatically authorize every separate email-tracking operation performed by that provider.

This does not always mean displaying a second cookie banner inside an email. Email has no normal banner workflow. It means the organization must determine the lawful and ePrivacy basis for the tracking, explain it clearly, and collect any required consent through an appropriate signup, preference, or consent process.

The European Data Protection Board's technical guidance specifically addresses URL and pixel tracking. It explains that:

  • A tracking pixel may be embedded in a website or an email to trigger a request back to its host.
  • A legitimate campaign image can also be used for tracking when additional identifying information is added to its URL.
  • A tracked link can collect an identifier when the recipient visits it.
  • Tracking pixels and tracked URLs can fall within Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive.

Article 5(3) generally requires consent after clear and comprehensive information, except for narrowly defined transmission and strictly necessary cases. Marketing measurement should not simply be assumed to qualify as strictly necessary.

Kooboo cannot make an organization's legal decisions automatically. What it can do is remove much of the unnecessary technical fragmentation around those decisions.

Keep the marketing operation inside your own Kooboo deployment

When Kooboo, the website, its customer data, and the email-marketing system run in the organization's chosen environment, the audience does not have to be uploaded to a separate marketing SaaS merely to send a campaign.

The organization can keep control of:

  • The original customer and consent records
  • The segmentation and campaign logic
  • The rendered message for every recipient
  • The tracking and delivery records
  • The retention and deletion policy
  • The server region and hosting provider
  • The SMTP or mail-transfer infrastructure used for delivery

For an EU-focused organization, Kooboo can be deployed on infrastructure located in the EU and operated under the organization's own account and policies. If the organization also operates its own mail-transfer service, it can avoid sending the marketing database and recipient-level campaign analytics to a separate email-marketing SaaS.

Using an external SMTP relay, cloud host, support service, or external database may still introduce processors and international transfers. The advantage is control and reduction, not a claim that installing Kooboo makes every deployment automatically GDPR-compliant.

Kooboo lets the business design one first-party data architecture instead of continuously reconciling the website with a second marketing data platform.

One campaign. A different result for every recipient.

Traditional personalization usually means replacing a few tokens:

Hello {FirstName}

That is useful, but it does not make the email truly dynamic. The structure, offer, products, content, and logic normally remain the same for everyone.

Kooboo takes the campaign HTML through its website rendering engine. Before an email is sent, Kooboo creates a rendering context for that recipient and makes the recipient and campaign links available to the template. Server-side code can prepare additional values, and the template can render the final HTML from the resulting context.

That makes it possible to vary much more than a name:

  • Show different content according to customer type, language, location, or account state.
  • Build product recommendations from the recipient's current data.
  • Display a different offer for a new customer, active customer, or inactive customer.
  • Generate links containing the correct recipient and campaign context.
  • Use server-side JavaScript to calculate, enrich, or retrieve values before rendering.
  • Change complete sections of the email instead of replacing isolated words.

Kooboo does not send one document to an entire list. It executes the campaign separately for each recipient.

Write an email with the power of a Kooboo web page

A campaign is still HTML, so a web developer starts with familiar technology. The important difference is that Kooboo does not treat that HTML as a static file.

The email body can use Kooboo's server-rendered template behavior, including data bindings and KScript. For example, a template can bind directly to the current recipient:

<h1>Hello, <span k-content="Contact.Name">customer</span></h1>

<p>We selected these recommendations for your account.</p>

<script env="server">
  // Run server-side JavaScript while Kooboo prepares this recipient's email.
  // Retrieve data, apply business rules, and expose the result to the template.
</script>

The server-side script is executed by Kooboo while generating the message. It is not delivered to the recipient's email client. The recipient receives the final rendered HTML.

This distinction matters. Email clients cannot safely run arbitrary application JavaScript, and their HTML support is more restricted than a modern browser. Kooboo gives the author a programmable server-side preparation stage, then produces email-compatible output for delivery.

A campaign may also define JavaScript hooks around the complete campaign and around each recipient. This allows the developer to prepare campaign-wide state once, enrich an individual recipient before rendering, or perform supported follow-up work after that recipient's content has been generated.

The development model stays familiar:

HTML for structure. CSS for presentation. JavaScript for logic. Kooboo data for the application.

The subject line is personal too

The first decision often happens before the email is opened. A dynamic body with a generic subject leaves much of the personalization unfinished.

Kooboo can render a recipient-specific subject from campaign and contact data. A subject such as:

{Contact.Name}, we selected something for you

is resolved for the individual recipient before sending. Campaign scripts can also prepare values that the subject and body use together, keeping the message consistent.

Kooboo supports A/B campaigns as well. Two campaign versions can use different content or subjects, and the winner can be selected by open or click performance. Personalization and experimentation therefore operate inside the same campaign system rather than through a second testing product.

Your website data is already the audience

In a conventional marketing stack, the website database and the email platform maintain separate versions of the customer. Every new field creates another mapping. Every update creates another synchronization event. Every failure creates the possibility that the marketing system acts on stale information.

Kooboo can use native contact lists stored in its own high-performance IndexedDB/B-tree storage. It can also create virtual lists by combining native lists and applying filters without copying every contact into another permanent list.

The campaign system can also read recipients from data that already belongs to a Kooboo website or application:

  • Kooboo structured content
  • Kooboo IndexedDB dynamic tables
  • SQLite databases
  • MySQL databases
  • SQL Server and supported SQL configurations

A remote-list configuration identifies the source website, database type, connection, table, key field, email field, and optional bounce and unsubscribe fields. Additional columns from the source record remain available as recipient data during rendering.

This creates a much shorter data path:

Application data → recipient context → rendered email

There is no required CSV export and no mandatory copy of the entire customer database into a separate email SaaS. When a campaign should use an external database, Kooboo can connect to it. When the data is already inside Kooboo, the campaign can use it where it lives.

Inspect the exact email that was generated

Previewing a template is not the same as proving what a particular person received.

A template preview may look correct while the real recipient data produces an empty field, an unexpected condition, a different subject, or a broken link. In many systems, the final personalized message disappears into the delivery provider after it is generated.

Kooboo keeps the generated recipient output with the campaign task. Depending on the campaign format, it can retain the individual:

  • Rendered HTML body
  • Rendered plain-text alternative
  • Rendered AMP body
  • Resolved subject line

The delivery preview reads that recipient-specific output. The user can choose a recipient and inspect the personalized subject and message that Kooboo actually generated—not merely reopen the original campaign template.

When a customer asks, “What did you send me?”, Kooboo can show the generated message, not an approximation.

This is useful for support, campaign quality control, and debugging. A developer can compare the source campaign with the output for one recipient and determine whether a problem came from the data, the template, the server-side logic, or delivery.

Delivery history is part of the campaign

Kooboo records recipient-level delivery information alongside the generated output. The record can include the recipient address, waiting or sent state, success or failure, send time, SMTP response code, and delivery log.

This joins three facts that are too often separated:

  1. Which person Kooboo intended to contact
  2. What Kooboo generated for that person
  3. What happened when Kooboo attempted delivery

That connection makes troubleshooting more direct. The operator can inspect the failed recipient, read the delivery result, and review the exact content that was prepared for the send.

First-party tracking without the usual third-party detour

A usable email system must handle more than composition and SMTP.

Kooboo's campaign pipeline supports click tracking, open tracking, bounce handling, spam-report handling, and unsubscribe processing. It can generate recipient-aware tracking and unsubscribe routes while preparing the email.

The implementation is different from the common external-platform pattern.

For open measurement, Kooboo does not append a separate invisible one-pixel image. It uses the first real HTML or CSS image resource already present in the campaign and gives that image a recipient-aware URL on the Kooboo website. When requested, Kooboo records the event and returns the actual image. If the campaign contains no image resource, there is no additional hidden tracking pixel to load.

External campaign images used for this purpose are downloaded into Kooboo's local campaign storage and served through the Kooboo site. The email client therefore does not need to contact the original external image host for the tracked image.

For click measurement, Kooboo creates a recipient-aware route under the website's own domain. When the destination is a page or resource on the same Kooboo site, Kooboo records the click and renders the local destination directly. It does not issue an extra HTTP 302 redirect to reach that local page. External destinations still require a redirect after the click has been recorded.

Compare the request paths:

Typical external platform:
Email client → external marketing tracker → redirect → website

Kooboo with a local destination:
Email client → your Kooboo domain → the requested page is rendered

This keeps the tracking endpoint, campaign record, and destination website under the same first-party domain and Kooboo runtime. It avoids sending every local click through an unrelated marketing domain.

It is still tracking. A real campaign image with a recipient identifier and a recipient-aware link remain subject to the organization's privacy and consent obligations. First-party architecture reduces third-party disclosure and international-transfer complexity; it does not remove the need for transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, retention rules, and any consent required by applicable law.

Messages include the standard one-click unsubscribe headers used by compatible email clients:

  • List-Unsubscribe
  • List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click

When recipients are collected for a campaign, Kooboo excludes contacts already marked as bounced or unsubscribed. Lists configured for double opt-in can also exclude contacts that have not confirmed. Duplicate addresses from combined lists are removed before sending.

For connected data sources, the contact-list mapping can identify bounce and unsubscribe fields in the original data. This lets the email system work with the application's own recipient state instead of maintaining an invisible copy that the application never sees.

These capabilities help implement a responsible email program, but the website owner still controls the campaign purpose, lawful basis, consent policy, retention policy, sender identity, and regional compliance requirements. Software can enforce configured rules; it cannot replace those business decisions.

Campaigns can become customer journeys

Some messages belong to a scheduled broadcast. Others should react to what the customer does.

Kooboo includes customer-journey automation with building blocks for triggers, conditions, delays, percentages, email actions, data enrichment, and webhooks. A journey can respond to application events and move a recipient through a controlled sequence.

Examples include:

  • Welcome a new member and follow up after a delay.
  • Send different onboarding content according to account type.
  • Remind a customer about an incomplete action.
  • Notify a user before a subscription or service period ends.
  • Enrich recipient data before selecting the next message.
  • Call a webhook as part of a broader business process.

Because the journey, recipient data, server-side logic, and website application can live in Kooboo, developers do not need to rebuild the same business state in a disconnected automation product.

Designed to generate at campaign scale

Rendering a unique email for every recipient is much more powerful than performing simple text replacement, but it also demands an efficient execution model.

Kooboo does not repeatedly parse the complete campaign from the beginning for every address. It evaluates the HTML, text, AMP, and dynamic subject into reusable render plans, freezes those plans for the send task, and then executes them against each recipient context.

The delivery system processes recipients in batches. Native lists can be scanned from serialized byte records, and supported virtual-list filters can evaluate against those records without first materializing every contact as a large object graph. External SQL sources are read in chunks. Generated recipient output is written directly to task storage.

The result is an architecture designed for both personalization and volume:

Prepare once → stream recipients → execute per person → store the result → send through pooled delivery connections

This is the same design philosophy found throughout Kooboo: keep the abstraction powerful, but make the execution path direct.

Use Kooboo delivery or your own SMTP

Owning the campaign should not force the sender into one delivery provider.

Kooboo can use its configured mail-transfer path or connect to a custom SMTP service. Custom settings include the host, port, SSL mode, credentials, connection concurrency, and the number of messages sent through a connection.

This separates two responsibilities cleanly:

  • Kooboo: audience selection, personalization, rendering, automation, generated-message history, tracking, and delivery records
  • The chosen mail service: transporting the message to the recipient's mail server

The business retains control of its website data and campaign logic while choosing the delivery infrastructure that fits its volume, geography, reputation strategy, and operational requirements.

If a third-party SMTP provider is selected, that provider and its processing locations must still be included in the organization's privacy and vendor review. Kooboo removes the requirement for a separate marketing database and campaign platform; it does not hide the delivery provider that the organization chooses.

Email is no longer an integration beside the website

The real advantage of Kooboo Email Marketing is not a longer feature checklist. It is the removal of boundaries.

  • The audience is not separated from the application data.
  • The email template is not separated from the website rendering engine.
  • The personalization logic is not limited to a handful of merge tags.
  • The subject is not separated from the recipient context.
  • The generated message is not separated from the delivery result.
  • The campaign is not separated from automation, A/B testing, bounce handling, and unsubscribe state.
  • The customer database does not have to be copied to a separate marketing SaaS.
  • Local email links do not have to redirect through a third-party tracking domain.
  • The sender is not locked to one SMTP provider.

Kooboo turns email from an external service that periodically receives exported customer data into a native capability of the website and application.

One website. One data model. One rendering engine. Every email personal.

Legal and technical sources

  • General Data Protection Regulation, especially Articles 28 and 44
  • ePrivacy Directive, especially Article 5(3)
  • EDPB Guidelines 2/2023 on the technical scope of Article 5(3)
  • European Commission guidance on international data transfers
  • Mailchimp Data Processing Addendum
  • Mailchimp explanation of open tracking
  • Mailchimp explanation of click redirects

Kooboo Email Marketing: Build the audience, logic, message, and customer journey where the business already runs.

Kooboo Multilingual

One Website. Every Language.

Enable it. Scan it. Translate it. Kooboo handles the routes, links, and SEO.

Turning an existing website into a multilingual website is usually treated as a new development project.

Teams duplicate pages, install translation plugins, redesign routes, rebuild navigation, create language-specific APIs, repair links that lose the selected language, and manually maintain SEO metadata for every translated URL.

Kooboo makes multilingual support part of the website itself.

Enable the languages, scan the existing site for translatable text, add the language switcher, and choose how language should appear in the URL. Kooboo then carries the active culture through rendering, content queries, links, routes, redirects, and search-engine metadata.

You do not rebuild the website for every language. You teach one website how to speak them all.

The complete workflow takes four steps

  1. Enable multilingual support and choose the languages.
  2. Scan the existing website and convert its text into translatable Labels.
  3. Add a language switcher using the built-in multilingual KScript API.
  4. Choose the URL strategy while Kooboo handles link rewriting and language SEO.

The important difference is that these are not four unrelated tools. They all use the same culture configuration and the same website objects.

Step one: enable multilingual support

Open the website’s Basic settings and enable Multilingual. Add the languages the website should support, give each language a readable display name, and choose the default language.

The same panel controls the important behavior:

  • Languages: the culture codes and names available to the website
  • Default language: the language used when no other culture is selected
  • Parameter mode: language is represented by a query parameter
  • Route mode: language is represented in the URL path
  • Default language prefix: whether the default language also appears in path-mode URLs
  • Auto-detect language: select a suitable culture for a new visitor
  • HrefLang: publish alternate-language information for search engines

Once the setting is saved, the website has one shared culture model. Pages, Labels, structured content, server rendering, routing, and KScript can all use the current language.

Step two: scan the website instead of finding every sentence manually

An existing website may contain hundreds or thousands of pieces of fixed text: headings, buttons, navigation labels, form hints, image descriptions, and messages. Finding and converting them by hand is one of the most expensive parts of multilingual migration.

Kooboo’s Label manager includes a site scanner.

Scan Labels inspects supported DOM-based website resources and identifies text that has not yet been connected to the translation system. It can discover:

  • Visible text inside HTML elements
  • title attributes
  • placeholder attributes
  • alt attributes
  • Text in Pages, Layouts, Views, and other supported DOM resources

The results show the source object, original value, attribute, and a suggested editable Label key. Select the items you want to translate and confirm the conversion.

Kooboo then does the structural work:

  • Creates the Label with the original text in the default language
  • Adds k-label to normal text elements
  • Adds a Label-backed binding for translatable attributes
  • Updates the original website object
  • Records the relationship between the Label and its source

The separate Scan I18N workflow finds existing t(...) translation calls inside supported DOM-based resources and can add missing Label entries. This is useful when parts of the site already use translation calls but the central Label collection is incomplete.

Kooboo does not ask you to remember where every sentence lives. It scans the website, shows you the candidates, and converts the approved text at its source.

One translation system for HTML, attributes, JavaScript, and APIs

Labels are designed for reusable interface copy: headings, buttons, field hints, status messages, short paragraphs, and other text that belongs to the website experience.

Each Label has one stable key and a value for every enabled language.

Translate normal HTML text

<h1 k-label="hero_title">Build for the whole world</h1>
<p k-label="hero_description">One website, every language.</p>
<a href="/contact" k-label="contact_us">Contact us</a>

During rendering, Kooboo replaces the element content with the value of that Label in the current culture.

Translate HTML attributes

Inputs and accessibility attributes need translated values too. Use k.label(...) through an attribute binding:

<input k-attribute="placeholder k.label('search_placeholder')">
<button k-attribute="aria-label k.label('open_menu')">
  <span aria-hidden="true">☰</span>
</button>

The same approach works for title, aria-label, alt, and other values that should follow the selected language.

Translate messages in server JavaScript and APIs

k.api.post((body) => {
  return {
    success: true,
    message: k.label("order_created", {
      orderNo: body.orderNo
    })
  };
});

Label values can contain parameters such as {name} or {orderNo}. Kooboo resolves the current language and inserts the runtime values before returning the message.

For existing literal text, k.t(...) provides a fast path into the same Label system. If the Label does not yet exist, the current implementation can create it automatically.

Step three: add a language switcher with one KScript API
